blocks.text: Apple’s dynamic configuration UI in their online store doesn’t hide or disguise the pricing or configuration options, but it doesn’t present all of the options at a glance. I find it useful to organize all of the configuration options into tables on a single page, and I figured it might be useful to share this now, before I finish writing my full thoughts on the redesigned hardware and displays for the PROLED XDR models.
Notes:

The old-style (mini-LED, no touchscreens, heavier) M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros were announced and began shipping in March 2026, alongside the new Studio Display and Studio Display XDR, the MacBook Neo, and M5 MacBook Airs.
The new but old-style plain 14-inch M6 MacBook Pro was announced in October 2026 and is set to begin shipping in early November.
The all-new PROLED XDR (touchscreens, lighter weight) M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pros were announced in October 2026 and are set to begin shipping in early November.

As in previous generations, there are no 16-inch models for the plain M6 or the chip-binned fewer-core M5 Pro configurations. The 16-inch MacBook Pro starts with the full 18-core CPU / 20-core GPU M5 Pro chip.
16-inch models, when available, cost $300 more than the same-specced 14-inch configuration.
Nano-texture displays are an option for all MacBook Pro models, and always cost $150.

articles.title: College will only cost $20 a month
articles.titleZh: College will only cost $20 a month
articles.summary: College will only cost $20 a month

blocks.text: From 2020 to 2022, I've encouraged a steady stream of students to pursue their education in computer science. Tech companies were hiring like crazy. I would interview 3 candidates a week on some occasions. The future of tech seemed to be paved with gold. Any day now, several of those students will graduate. I dread opening my inbox and get an email from them asking:
"So... about those jobs?"

Things have changed since those crazy old days. Hiring has come to a stop. Those graduates will step into a market that looks nothing like what they signed up for. Getting a job will be a struggle. If I could see the future, I would have recommended a different path. But then again, how could I have known? Hindsight is always 20/20.

So this leaves me with a dilemma as a parent. What do I tell my own kids? Am I going to push them to pursue the same traditional colleges? Will I disburse life savings so they could attend a prestigious university? Or will I just buy them a $20 a month AI Subscription?

Imagine handing a student a textbook straight from a university syllabus. They read a lesson, and then you have an AI tutor to quiz them, debate concepts, and break down difficult ideas until they fully grasp the material. Is that a good replacement for college?

Some argue that college is about the experience. It's the friendships you make along the way, the networking, the independence. These same people often omit the lifetime of crippling debt that hangs over those friends twenty years later.

When I was in college, I focused almost entirely on mastering the material in the books, completing all assignments quickly. I spent the rest of the semesters tutoring my peers and applying the material I had learned. For me replacing the entire college system, the brick-and-mortar university with a set of books and an AI subscription seems like it would have done the job. I was the target candidate for this model.
Yet, now that I have these AIs to experiment it myself, I found two flaws in the model:
Understanding takes time.
Not having an immediate answer forces you to strain your brain until you figure things out.

When I wrestled with dense textbooks in college, solutions didn't arrive at the click of a button. Instead, I struggled. I hit dead ends. I tried solutions that seemed promising only to abruptly stop two hours in the process only to realize that the whole thing was wrong. Sitting with the problem, the trials, the errors, giving up and going for a walk to clear my head, that was the process that taught me how to think. It taught me how to debug.

Even when I found solutions online and pasted them into my code, I had to encounter the same problem repeatedly before the concept finally made sense. You have to work your way through a solution to understand a problem.

This is why I feel concerned when we throw Millennium Prize Mathematical problems at AI. Imagine an AI presents a complete proof to one of these unsolved problems tomorrow? If or when AI solves it, we still have two problems.
We still have to understand the solution. Having an AI produce a proof doesn't mean we understand how or why it works.
We don't get to discover new problems.

The second one is often overlooked, but ask yourself, where do these problems in Mathematics come from? They come from mathematicians attempting to solve hard problems, taking detours and failing along the way. Remove that step, and you... Well, you don't find any new problems.

Not just in mathematics, I feel we will see something similar in code where fewer applications rely on frameworks. Frameworks solve real issues in programming, but why use a framework when the AI can just give you all the answers. I lived through the JS framework mania. I am not suggesting we create more, but I think we will miss out on discovering new problems that need solving.
If we rely on a system that just hands us a solution, we lose the ability to uncover new questions because we never went through the steps of trying something new.

I don't think a $20-a-month AI subscription paired with a textbook is the ultimate solution. Not when we still need some friction in order to inculcate concepts in our minds. But traditional higher education has changed so drastically and the skyrocketing costs and changing employment realities don’t help. There is no turning back to the old model either.

The challenge for learning remains understanding. How we grasp concepts and develop critical thinking in an era of instant answers. Maybe that's where we should turn our focus to. Figuring out how to design learning that somehow preserves productive struggle. If AI can solve this issue and turn students into masters of crafts instead of prompt engineers, I mean, I'll gladly keep that college tuition in my pocket.

Formalities (permalink)

It's not often that I find myself on the same side as the US Copyright Office. In fact, I think this is the first time in 25 years that I've found myself cheering on the office's official actions as good for art and good for free expression, taking the side of creative workers over our bosses.

The source of our miraculous accord: the US Copyright Office's position on AI. The CO has taken the (entirely correct) position that copyright law exists to incentivize human acts of creative expression, which means that only works of human authorship are eligible for copyright.

This isn't a controversial position within legal circles. But for media executives, this is shocking; absurd, even. This gap between the industrial and the legal understanding of copyright comes from a fundamental difference over the evocatively named legal doctrine of "sweat of the brow."

"Sweat of the brow" is fundamental to a correct legal understanding of copyright. Copyright rewards and protects creativity but it does not protect hard work. You can labor for ten years over a phone book listing the numbers of every person in a town and (as a collection of uncopyrightable facts) it will receive no protection at all. Zero. Zilch. Anyone can copy and sell that phone book:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feist_Publications,_Inc._v._Rural_Telephone_Service_Co.

Copyright law doesn't care if you slaved over that collection of facts, if you missed sleep and your kids' little league games to realize your grand vision. Copyright law doesn't care if you plowed every cent into it, remortgaging your home and cashing in your (already resentful) kids' college funds.

But: if you dash off a haiku in ten seconds while sitting on the toilet, shove it into your pocket and forget about it, and then your (still resentful) kids discover that crumpled haiku after your (highly suspicious) death, your kids will be able to claim a full 70 years' worth of copyright over that forgotten triviality (the term of copyright for works of human authorship is life plus 70 years).

This is the uncontroversial and universally accepted legal understanding of copyright: all the copyright in the world for creative acts, no copyright at all for mere acts of labor. The "sweat of the brow" has nothing to do with a work's eligibility for copyright.

But no media boss believes this. For media bosses, copyright is a pseudo-property† right, designed and operated to protect their bottom line. The point of copyright isn't to incentivize creativity, but rather investment.
† Or not-so-pseudo

There's obviously a relationship between creative acts and acts of investment, but it's possible to create without investment (see: your haiku) and it's possible to invest without creativity (see: your phone book).

And once again, the creativity that copyright protects is human creativity. This is a lesson that David Slater learned the hard way. Slater is a professional wildlife photographer and amateur monkey-trainer who combined his interests by teaching Celebes crested macaque monkeys to take selfies. But when Slater published a monkey's selfie others copied and distributed the image without his permission, on the (entirely legally correct) basis that monkeys are not humans, and that means that works created by monkeys don't get a copyright. This was also the Copyright Office's position, and the position of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey_selfie_copyright_dispute

This is the basis for the US Copyright Office's repeated decision to refuse to extend copyright to AI-generated works. An algorithm is even less human than a monkey, so if you can't get copyright over a monkey selfie, you definitely can't copyright your chatbot's slop. The US Copyright Office has successfully defended this position in multiple courts, triumphing over plaintiffs who were so persistent that they even got the Supreme Court to weigh in on the issue (the Supremes decided the case didn't warrant their attention):
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation

AI slop isn't copyrightable, but there can be copyrightable elements in an AI-generated image. The most obvious element is the prompt. So long as your prompt contains some quantum of creativity (e.g. "Make me a beautiful flower whose loveliness is reminiscent of a newborn baby", but not "make me a beautiful flower"), that prompt is copyrightable. That means you can use copyright to challenge others' rights to present the same prompt to a chatbot. But while the prompt can be copyrighted, the image it gives rise to isn't. So you can spend a month iteratively refining your prompt, consuming all your town's water along with 200,000 gallons of diesel and that prompt will be yours for your life plus 70 years, but the image it generates is in the public domain, and anyone can copy it, sell it or give it away.

There are other ways that copyright can find its way into AI-generated material. You can make creative edits to it: if you output a slop novel and rewrite various sentences (providing those rewrites involve some creativity and not just mechanical corrections or word substitutions), then the edited sentences become copyrighted works, even though all the rest of the text remains uncopyrightable.

You can also get a "thin" copyright through selection. If you get your chatbot to output many images based on your prompt and choose your favorite, your selection can confer a tiny bit of copyright over that creative act of selection, but it will be harder to defend than even the other (attenuated and highly specific) forms of copyright.

Now, perhaps you've spotted an administrative problem lurking in this turn of events. How can someone else know what part of a work is AI-generated (and thus in the public domain) and which parts are human-edited/contributed (and thus copyrighted)? Just as importantly, how can you prove which parts of your work are not AI-generated and thus eligible for copyright protection.

This gets especially gnarly when you're dealing with complex media. In an animation, an AI might do the rigging and movement for a human-created sprite. The sprite is copyrightable, but its movements aren't. That would mean that I could remap your sprite's movements onto a different sprite without infringing your copyright. Or say the sprite and its movements are human created (and thus copyrighted), but the backgrounds are procedurally generated? I could take those backgrounds and put new animations overtop of them.

The simplest, most reliable way to ensure the works you invest in are fully and entirely eligible for copyright is to just use humans for the whole project. Declare a "no-AI policy," and hire human artists to produce the works you hope to sell. Monitor their activity to ensure they're not using AI. Keep good records.

Now, as much as I like the idea that we've arrived at a copyright law that insists that a company can only get exclusive rights to its products by paying human artists to make them from end-to-end, I don't think that's likely to be the way it shakes out, but that doesn't mean that this is a wash for artists.

The reality is that copyright claims are always "fact-intensive inquiries" that are expensive to litigate and difficult to adjudicate. It's completely normal for copyright lawsuits to turn on documentary evidence gleaned from fragmentary records. This is simply intrinsic to copyright, because copyright is a doctrine that requires judges to assess whether things are "creative" and "original" as though these were freestanding categories that everyone could agree upon.

Of course, the rules of copyright can make this harder or easier. One way in which the rules make deciding copyright cases much, much harder is copyright's broad prohibition on "formalities" ("formalities" is how copyright wonks refer to "red tape" or "paperwork"). For nearly all of American history, copyright ran on a key formality: deposit, registration and notice.

To secure a copyright for a new work, an artist (or their employer) had to send a copy of that work to the Library of Congress (deposit), along with paperwork detailing the claim of authorship (who made this, what parts of it did they make) (registration) and they had to display a copyright notice that told you who held the copyright to every work that was registered (notice). Both the filing and the notice required careful attention and precision, and screwing either one up could result in your losing your copyright. It's an open secret among copyright scholars that Walt Disney screwed this up with the first Mickey cartoons, meaning they've been in the public domain since their release:
https://web.archive.org/web/20080725055415/http:/homepages.law.asu.edu/~dkarjala/opposingcopyrightextension/publicdomain/HedenkampFreeMickeyMouseVaSp&E(2003).htm

This system of copyright formalities meant that you could always tell whether a work was copyrighted, you could always find out who claimed the copyright over it, and which parts of the work were claimed under copyright and under what basis. What's more, formalities created the Library of Congress, since the LoC acted as America's "copyright deposit" library, holding deposit copies of every work that had ever been issued a US copyright.

The US system of formalities was descended from the English system, in which the Stationers' Guild used a copyright registry to establish who had the rights to which books. But there were competing copyright systems, notably the "continental" system that was codified through the Berne Convention, a copyright treaty drafted by Victor Hugo (yes, that Victor Hugo).

Among other things, the Berne Convention abolished formalities. Much of the world adopted Berne, but the US held out until 1976. With the 1976 Copyright Act, Congress brought the US into compliance with Berne, abolishing formalities in the USA. As a compromise, the 1976 Act requires US authors to register their copyrights in order to obtain "statutory damages" (up to $150,000 per work). That's a pretty good incentive, but even with that incentive, the vast majority – far in excess of 99.999999999999999999999999999999999999999% – of all copyrighted works are not registered with the Copyright Office. They are born copyrighted from the moment they are "fixed in a tangible medium" until 70 years after their authors die. But without registration, you can't know when that copyright clock started ticking because you have no way to verify who the author of the work is. This not only makes it incredibly difficult to establish the copyright status of nearly every copyrighted work, but it also means that in nearly every case, you can't readily determine who you should approach if you want to pay them for a copyright license.

Abolishing formalities has created a universe of orphan works: everything from napkin doodles to kindergartners' finger paintings to message board posts. Within that universe is a kind of gaseous cloud that, if condensed, would come out to an infinitesimal planetoid, representing the entirety of commercial works whose authors give a damn about their copyright status. It's a bad, bad system.

This system doesn't do away with the need to keep careful records: like I said, copyright disputes usually require the close examination of documentary evidence. What formality abolition accomplished was the destruction of the regular system of record-keeping: rather than having a standard, universally agreed-upon way to determine the status and resolve disputes about a copyrighted work, now we have the scattershot, incoherent system that makes copyright disputes far more likely (because no one knows who to approach for copyright licenses) and far more difficult to resolve (because there's no registry of copyrighted works).

Which brings me back to the question of AI and copyright. If a firm uses some AI in its work, it's going to need to document that very carefully. Firms that don't keep very close track of the elements of their products that come from AI will have a far harder time defending their commercial interests.

Basically, we're about to recreate formalities, but managed by the private sector. To the extent that companies use AI in their work, they are going to have to track every pixel and every word and every note that is output by an AI system, and which parts were added or edited by humans after creation.

It's not often that I find myself on the same side as the US Copyright Office. In fact, I think this is the first time in 25 years that I've found myself cheering on the office's official actions as good for art and good for free expression, taking the side of creative workers over our bosses.

The source of our miraculous accord: the US Copyright Office's position on AI. The CO has taken the (entirely correct) position that copyright law exists to incentivize human acts of creative expression, which means that only works of human authorship are eligible for copyright.

This isn't a controversial position within legal circles. But for media executives, this is shocking; absurd, even. This gap between the industrial and the legal understanding of copyright comes from a fundamental difference over the evocatively named legal doctrine of "sweat of the brow."

"Sweat of the brow" is fundamental to a correct legal understanding of copyright. Copyright rewards and protects creativity but it does not protect hard work. You can labor for ten years over a phone book listing the numbers of every person in a town and (as a collection of uncopyrightable facts) it will receive no protection at all. Zero. Zilch. Anyone can copy and sell that phone book:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feist_Publications,_Inc._v._Rural_Telephone_Service_Co.

Copyright law doesn't care if you slaved over that collection of facts, if you missed sleep and your kids' little league games to realize your grand vision. Copyright law doesn't care if you plowed every cent into it, remortgaging your home and cashing in your (already resentful) kids' college funds.

But: if you dash off a haiku in ten seconds while sitting on the toilet, shove it into your pocket and forget about it, and then your (still resentful) kids discover that crumpled haiku after your (highly suspicious) death, your kids will be able to claim a full 70 years' worth of copyright over that forgotten triviality (the term of copyright for works of human authorship is life plus 70 years).

This is the uncontroversial and universally accepted legal understanding of copyright: all the copyright in the world for creative acts, no copyright at all for mere acts of labor. The "sweat of the brow" has nothing to do with a work's eligibility for copyright.

But no media boss believes this. For media bosses, copyright is a pseudo-property† right, designed and operated to protect their bottom line. The point of copyright isn't to incentivize creativity, but rather investment.
† Or not-so-pseudo

There's obviously a relationship between creative acts and acts of investment, but it's possible to create without investment (see: your haiku) and it's possible to invest without creativity (see: your phone book).

And once again, the creativity that copyright protects is human creativity. This is a lesson that David Slater learned the hard way. Slater is a professional wildlife photographer and amateur monkey-trainer who combined his interests by teaching Celebes crested macaque monkeys to take selfies. But when Slater published a monkey's selfie others copied and distributed the image without his permission, on the (entirely legally correct) basis that monkeys are not humans, and that means that works created by monkeys don't get a copyright. This was also the Copyright Office's position, and the position of the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monkey_selfie_copyright_dispute

This is the basis for the US Copyright Office's repeated decision to refuse to extend copyright to AI-generated works. An algorithm is even less human than a monkey, so if you can't get copyright over a monkey selfie, you definitely can't copyright your chatbot's slop. The US Copyright Office has successfully defended this position in multiple courts, triumphing over plaintiffs who were so persistent that they even got the Supreme Court to weigh in on the issue (the Supremes decided the case didn't warrant their attention):
https://pluralistic.net/2026/03/03/its-a-trap-2/#inheres-at-the-moment-of-fixation

AI slop isn't copyrightable, but there can be copyrightable elements in an AI-generated image. The most obvious element is the prompt. So long as your prompt contains some quantum of creativity (e.g. "Make me a beautiful flower whose loveliness is reminiscent of a newborn baby", but not "make me a beautiful flower"), that prompt is copyrightable. That means you can use copyright to challenge others' rights to present the same prompt to a chatbot. But while the prompt can be copyrighted, the image it gives rise to isn't. So you can spend a month iteratively refining your prompt, consuming all your town's water along with 200,000 gallons of diesel and that prompt will be yours for your life plus 70 years, but the image it generates is in the public domain, and anyone can copy it, sell it or give it away.

There are other ways that copyright can find its way into AI-generated material. You can make creative edits to it: if you output a slop novel and rewrite various sentences (providing those rewrites involve some creativity and not just mechanical corrections or word substitutions), then the edited sentences become copyrighted works, even though all the rest of the text remains uncopyrightable.

You can also get a "thin" copyright through selection. If you get your chatbot to output many images based on your prompt and choose your favorite, your selection can confer a tiny bit of copyright over that creative act of selection, but it will be harder to defend than even the other (attenuated and highly specific) forms of copyright.

Now, perhaps you've spotted an administrative problem lurking in this turn of events. How can someone else know what part of a work is AI-generated (and thus in the public domain) and which parts are human-edited/contributed (and thus copyrighted)? Just as importantly, how can you prove which parts of your work are not AI-generated and thus eligible for copyright protection.

This gets especially gnarly when you're dealing with complex media. In an animation, an AI might do the rigging and movement for a human-created sprite. The sprite is copyrightable, but its movements aren't. That would mean that I could remap your sprite's movements onto a different sprite without infringing your copyright. Or say the sprite and its movements are human created (and thus copyrighted), but the backgrounds are procedurally generated? I could take those backgrounds and put new animations overtop of them.

The simplest, most reliable way to ensure the works you invest in are fully and entirely eligible for copyright is to just use humans for the whole project. Declare a "no-AI policy," and hire human artists to produce the works you hope to sell. Monitor their activity to ensure they're not using AI. Keep good records.

Now, as much as I like the idea that we've arrived at a copyright law that insists that a company can only get exclusive rights to its products by paying human artists to make them from end-to-end, I don't think that's likely to be the way it shakes out, but that doesn't mean that this is a wash for artists.

The reality is that copyright claims are always "fact-intensive inquiries" that are expensive to litigate and difficult to adjudicate. It's completely normal for copyright lawsuits to turn on documentary evidence gleaned from fragmentary records. This is simply intrinsic to copyright, because copyright is a doctrine that requires judges to assess whether things are "creative" and "original" as though these were freestanding categories that everyone could agree upon.

Of course, the rules of copyright can make this harder or easier. One way in which the rules make deciding copyright cases much, much harder is copyright's broad prohibition on "formalities" ("formalities" is how copyright wonks refer to "red tape" or "paperwork"). For nearly all of American history, copyright ran on a key formality: deposit, registration and notice.

To secure a copyright for a new work, an artist (or their employer) had to send a copy of that work to the Library of Congress (deposit), along with paperwork detailing the claim of authorship (who made this, what parts of it did they make) (registration) and they had to display a copyright notice that told you who held the copyright to every work that was registered (notice). Both the filing and the notice required careful attention and precision, and screwing either one up could result in your losing your copyright. It's an open secret among copyright scholars that Walt Disney screwed this up with the first Mickey cartoons, meaning they've been in the public domain since their release:
https://web.archive.org/web/20080725055415/http:/homepages.law.asu.edu/~dkarjala/opposingcopyrightextension/publicdomain/HedenkampFreeMickeyMouseVaSp&E(2003).htm

This system of copyright formalities meant that you could always tell whether a work was copyrighted, you could always find out who claimed the copyright over it, and which parts of the work were claimed under copyright and under what basis. What's more, formalities created the Library of Congress, since the LoC acted as America's "copyright deposit" library, holding deposit copies of every work that had ever been issued a US copyright.

The US system of formalities was descended from the English system, in which the Stationers' Guild used a copyright registry to establish who had the rights to which books. But there were competing copyright systems, notably the "continental" system that was codified through the Berne Convention, a copyright treaty drafted by Victor Hugo (yes, that Victor Hugo).

Among other things, the Berne Convention abolished formalities. Much of the world adopted Berne, but the US held out until 1976. With the 1976 Copyright Act, Congress brought the US into compliance with Berne, abolishing formalities in the USA. As a compromise, the 1976 Act requires US authors to register their copyrights in order to obtain "statutory damages" (up to $150,000 per work). That's a pretty good incentive, but even with that incentive, the vast majority – far in excess of 99.999999999999999999999999999999999999999% – of all copyrighted works are not registered with the Copyright Office. They are born copyrighted from the moment they are "fixed in a tangible medium" until 70 years after their authors die. But without registration, you can't know when that copyright clock started ticking because you have no way to verify who the author of the work is. This not only makes it incredibly difficult to establish the copyright status of nearly every copyrighted work, but it also means that in nearly every case, you can't readily determine who you should approach if you want to pay them for a copyright license.

Abolishing formalities has created a universe of orphan works: everything from napkin doodles to kindergartners' finger paintings to message board posts. Within that universe is a kind of gaseous cloud that, if condensed, would come out to an infinitesimal planetoid, representing the entirety of commercial works whose authors give a damn about their copyright status. It's a bad, bad system.

This system doesn't do away with the need to keep careful records: like I said, copyright disputes usually require the close examination of documentary evidence. What formality abolition accomplished was the destruction of the regular system of record-keeping: rather than having a standard, universally agreed-upon way to determine the status and resolve disputes about a copyrighted work, now we have the scattershot, incoherent system that makes copyright disputes far more likely (because no one knows who to approach for copyright licenses) and far more difficult to resolve (because there's no registry of copyrighted works).

Which brings me back to the question of AI and copyright. If a firm uses some AI in its work, it's going to need to document that very carefully. Firms that don't keep very close track of the elements of their products that come from AI will have a far harder time defending their commercial interests.

Basically, we're about to recreate formalities, but managed by the private sector. To the extent that companies use AI in their work, they are going to have to track every pixel and every word and every note that is output by an AI system, and which parts were added or edited by humans after creation.

That means that companies that want to protect their commercial interests aren't just going to get more protection based on how much work they get humans to do; they're also going to have to treat copyright's government-enforceable monopoly over expressive speech with the gravitas it deserves: not something you get automatically, but something you have to do real administrative work for.

articles.summary: Gig Review: The Witcher in Concert ★★★★☆

blocks.text: The most common way people experience classical style music these days is via movies and video-games. After seeing The Force Awakens - live in concert, I've become rather a fan of watching movies performed with a live soundtrack.
But what about watching a video game with orchestral accompaniment? We travelled up to Wolverhampton to see "The Witcher":
A one-of-a-kind live event that transforms the lasting legacy and emotional storytelling of The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt into an immersive concert

Obviously you can't have someone sat there with a PS5 controller while a band plays (although that'd be a hell of a Twitch stream!) instead a large screen projects various cut-scenes and in-game footage.  It works pretty well - most of the popular scenes are in there (Geralt in the bathtub got a big cheer) although there was no hyper-extended Gwent session. The videos were a little repetitive. Some of the music is obviously composed to be swelling in the background and so repeated shots of swords looking cool or Geralt looking grumpy were sprinkled throughout.

The highlight was seeing Percival Schuttenbach play a variety of instruments with absolute joy and gusto. The entire band look like they're having a whale of a time, and the conductor encouraged us to whoop and cheer for our favourite scenes (with perhaps a few boos for some of the more notorious enemies).

As soundtracks go, it isn't particularly varied. There's a decent mix of tunes, some with singing, but they do tend to blur into one after a while. Nevertheless, a brilliant time for fans of the game who want to soak up the music.
The Witcher in Concert is on tour around the world now.
Pre- and Post-Show

There was a merchandise stall hidden in one corner of the venue. Between doors opening and the start of the show (about an hour) a video looped through three screens - one of which encouraged up to share our photos with a hashtag. That's fine, but a few more videos wouldn't have gone amiss.
After the show, the conductor said the band would stick around for selfies - which was nice of them.

A touring show like this probably can't spare too much space for large scale models for people to pose with, or a couple of cosplayers to photograph, but it might have been nice if there were something to interact with before and after the show.

blocks.text: Happy Halloween! Here’s a little of what I got up to in this spooky month.
Things I did in October

I moved this site from an Apache-powered VPS to CDN-frontend object storage. This means I pay less money, I do less maintenance, and my site loads faster in most parts of the world. Hopefully nobody noticed this change, except that things should be a little snappier! (Also, my old site had a small amount of PHP, which I’m happy to have removed given PHP’s remote code execution vulnerabilities this month.)
In an effort to fill in the gaps of the internet, I published a short list of Vim forks.
At Ghost, my team shipped two additions to our automations feature: analytics and more granular triggers. Both of these should help our independent publishers grow. More automations stuff on the way!
Like every month, I wrote a few articles at Zelda Dungeon, including a debate over, perhaps, the most trivial disagreement possible.
Tech links I clicked on
The surveillance state takes another step: pinpointing addresses based on interior photos. Thanks, AI!
“How Technology Empowers—and Imperils—Dictators” is a reminder that technologists have a social duty.
Two lists of tech fascists: “Fashware” and “Weird little guys of FOSS”.
Continued to love David Rosenthal’s blog about the (seemingly unsustainable) economics of AI companies.
“Keyboard differences between Windows and Macs” is a deep dive into Control and Command and Copilot keys.
Data centers are unpopular, a problem Amazon is trying to spend its way out of.

“Programming Isn’t Special” argues that programming is art, and that most art isn’t “mystical”, and that using AI to do art has disadvantages. “If we use AI to erase all the copy-writing, all the graphic design, all the boring mundane art, and yes, all the boring custom WordPress theme development, then we will be removing all the practical opportunities for the vast amounts of practice and contemplation required for people to elevate their craft to eventually achieve great things.”
A fun AGENTS.md that says, “All LLM contributions are strictly forbidden.”
Other miscellany
Part biography, part memoir, part hopeful, part depressing…Why Fish Don’t Exist captivated me this month.
I plan to consult The Ultimate List of DRM-free Bookshops next time I buy an ebook.
Bookmarked this list of “every weird film ever (with a special emphasis on trash)”.
As a lifelong Diddy Kong Racing fan, I felt personally insulted by “Bloke Who Preferred The Thinking Man’s Mario Kart Growing Up Also A Weird Contrarian In Other Aspects Of His Strange Life”.
Hope you had a good October.

blocks.text: This week’s package management news, gathered from the package manager OPML feed collection, my posts and boosts on Mastodon, and anything people sent me.
Security

The Go blog’s eMudhra post-incident writeup covers Go’s first URGENT-track security release: Mozilla added eight eMudhra intermediates to OneCRL on 17 October, the Go security team was alerted on 19 October, and Go 1.27.3 and 1.26.10 shipped under seven and a half hours later with a patch that rejects any chain through those intermediates. The post also says Go plans to add revocation checking on Linux. A test page shows the git, curl and python3 that Apple ships with macOS still trusted the eMudhra intermediates on 28 October, and macOS 27.2 undid the workaround users had applied by hand.

sbt 1.13.1 and 2.0.12 fix a zip slip in IO.unzip and its variants (GHSA-p8jf-532w-4p65) that an earlier fix missed. pipx 1.18.7 now requires pip 26.2.2 or later in its shared libraries and replaces an older shared pip on the next pipx command instead of waiting for the 30-day refresh.
Releases

Composer 2.11 adds a cooldown dependency policy that withholds newly published versions for a configured period during update and require, with a --no-cooldown flag for installing a security fix straight away. It also removes the source fallback deprecated in 2.10 and lets custom policies block during composer install. 2.11.1 fixes GitLab CI job tokens against GitLab’s Composer registry.

pnpm 12.16 adds a global --env-file flag and fixes two security issues, one in zstd decompression and one in signing. 12.17 adds pnpm peers check --global and dependency-group selectors and wildcards in overrides, and pnpm outdated and pnpm update now cover runtime and package manager versions plus Cargo and Python dependencies. 11.28.9 fixes a crash on registry responses with too many content encodings (GHSA-xjj6-f33q-929c) and sizes the install worker pool from the container’s CPU quota.
Homebrew 7.0.11 verifies formula patch downloads from the API and requires verifiable sources for official formulae.

mise 2026.10.21 to 2026.10.25 adds mise bootstrap --config-dir so mise’s global config can be kept in a dotfiles checkout, deploys Stow-style packages without a per-package table, and lets mise bootstrap packages prune --force remove casks it cannot prove are unchanged.
Hatch 1.18.2 and Hatchling 1.33.0 support Python 3.15. Hatch’s managed 3.15 distributions are now the final 3.15.0 release, and the default test matrix includes 3.15 and the free-threaded 3.15t.

ORAS 1.3.6 narrows the bearer-realm denylist that 1.3.5 introduced. 1.3.5 rejected realms on any private address, which broke self-hosted split-host registries such as GitLab. The default now blocks only loopback, link-local, unspecified and cloud metadata addresses.
Harbor 2.16.0-rc1 replaces Redis with Valkey as the cache backend and builds for amd64 and arm64. It also proxies the referrers API to the upstream registry with paging and local merge.

Conan 2.34.0 makes a third fewer local cache database calls on installs from cache, sends original URLs to backup source remotes in an X-Conan-Origin-Urls header, and adds a command_alias.conf file for command shortcuts.
Gradle 9.9.0 RC1 keeps wrapper settings when upgrading the wrapper, filters non-method JUnit Platform tests, and compiles Kotlin DSL scripts faster.

Debcraft 1.0 (Otto Kekäläinen) builds Debian packages in a Podman or Docker container made from the suite in debian/changelog and the build dependencies in debian/control. It diffs the artifacts between two builds and automates importing new upstream versions.

Renovate 44.189.0 applies vulnerability alerts to transitive dependencies, opening security updates that change only the lockfile. 44.194.0 adds a manager for Paket, the .NET dependency manager. 44.184.0 reports gh actions-lock findings when the command fails and re-pins only the updated refs in actions.lock.
Also out:
RubyGems 4.1.0.beta3
setup-uv 10.3.3
sbt 2.1.0-RC2
Chocolatey 2.7.5 and 1.4.8
PSResourceGet 1.3.0-rc2
vcpkg tool 2026-10-29
Verdaccio 7.0.2
EasyBuild 5.4.2
Podman 6.2.0-rc1
Terraform 1.17.1
OpenTofu 1.13.5
Dependabot Core 0.402.0
Articles

tar-codec (William Woodruff, Astral) is a new Rust tar library and uv’s default tar reader as of 0.13. It is roughly twice as fast as the previous reader and reduces the risk of parser differentials: it refuses archives whose headers mix tar families, allows at most one GNU long-name and one long-link record per member, and refuses pax tombstones. UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1 restores the old reader.

A consistent(-ish) npm dependency graph (Evert Pot, vlt) finds that 22% of new npm versions in a 24-hour window arrived with at least one dependency still missing from the registry. vlt’s npm replication now holds a publish until its transitive dependencies are also available, and releases anything still held after an hour.

PyPI now limits versions to 128 characters. Two of the roughly 9.9 million releases on PyPI have a version that long, half have five characters or fewer, and 99% have twenty or fewer. Projects owned by a PyPI organisation now get higher default limits: 200 MB per file instead of 100 MB, 20 GB per project instead of 10 GB, and ten new projects per day.

How to fund Rust contributors (Jakub Beránek, Rust Blog) sets out three routes: the Rust Foundation Maintainers Fund or RustNL Maintainers Team for general maintenance, fundable Rust Project Goals for specific features, and GitHub Sponsors for individual contributors.

Ruby Central’s OSS Changelog is back after a long gap. RubyGems.org now validates gem pushes against a schema built from the metadata of all 180,000+ published gems, and it revoked every legacy API key after a report that its CDN could cache that endpoint’s responses and serve them to the wrong user. The Gem Security team has scanned about 317 of 619 heavily downloaded gems with AI models. Reviewers rejected 120 of 134 findings, and one that survived was a critical password check bug in rubyntlm, fixed in 0.6.6.

Thirteen backlogs in a trenchcoat (Jamie Tanna) sorts Renovate’s open backlog of 1,688 ideas, 1,005 issues and 465 human-authored PRs into 13 buckets of work. Renovate’s own bot opened 59% of the project’s pull requests in 2025.
Papers

The Policies of Programming Language Ecosystems (Jukka Ruohonen et al., arXiv) codes the published policies of eight package registries against 38 categories. All eight cover malware, intellectual property and content removal, while treatment of package size limits, metric manipulation, typo-squatting and binary uploads varies.

Supply Chain Insecurity: Exposing Vulnerabilities in iOS Dependency Management Systems (David Schmidt et al., arXiv) finds that iOS apps expose internal CocoaPods package names, which attackers can then register to run code on developer machines and build servers. Across 9,212 apps, hijacking a single CocoaPod through an abandoned domain could have compromised 63 of them.
Elsewhere

The call for participation for the Package Management devroom at FOSDEM 2027 is open until 1 December. I’m co-organising with Vlad Miricioiu, Wolf Vollprecht and Travis Hathaway. The Ruby devroom is also back for the first time in several years.
EasyBuild has joined the High Performance Software Foundation at the Core stage, the highest of HPSF’s three project stages.

Michał Górny’s The next circle of security hell is a follow-up to his 2021 “modern packager’s security nightmare” post, on vulnerability report volume and projects that bundle security fixes with feature and API changes.
Josh Bressers wrote up curl’s new policy of handling low and medium severity reports in public, covered here last week, and argues other projects should adopt it.
git-pkgs
I tagged 6 repos this week:
purl2swhid v0.1.0 (new), which turns a Package URL into a Software Heritage identifier and can request archival through Save Code Now
skills v0.2.0 (new), a Go library for finding and parsing Agent Skills in checkouts and package archives
typosquatting v0.1.0 (new), a Go library that generates package-name variants and checks names against a supplied corpus for PyPI, npm, RubyGems, Cargo, Go and GitHub Actions
enrichment v0.7.5
purl v0.2.1
registries v0.13.0

Hatch 1.18.2 and Hatchling 1.33.0 support Python 3.15. Hatch’s managed 3.15 distributions are now the final 3.15.0 release, and the default test matrix includes 3.15 and the free-threaded 3.15t.

ORAS 1.3.6 narrows the bearer-realm denylist that 1.3.5 introduced. 1.3.5 rejected realms on any private address, which broke self-hosted split-host registries such as GitLab. The default now blocks only loopback, link-local, unspecified and cloud metadata addresses.

Conan 2.34.0 makes a third fewer local cache database calls on installs from cache, sends original URLs to backup source remotes in an X-Conan-Origin-Urls header, and adds a command_alias.conf file for command shortcuts.
Gradle 9.9.0 RC1 keeps wrapper settings when upgrading the wrapper, filters non-method JUnit Platform tests, and compiles Kotlin DSL scripts faster.

Articles

UV_LEGACY_TAR_BACKEND=1 restores the old reader.

Papers

The Policies of Programming Language Ecosystems (Jukka Ruohonen et al., arXiv) codes the published policies of eight package registries against 38 categories. Across 9,212 apps, hijacking a single CocoaPod through an abandoned domain could have compromised 63 of them.

EasyBuild has joined the High Performance Software Foundation at the Core stage, the highest of HPSF’s three project stages.

Michał Górny’s The next circle of security hell is a follow-up to his 2021 “modern packager’s security nightmare” post, on vulnerability report volume and projects that bundle security fixes with feature and API changes.

blocks.text: Welcome to the reading list, a weekly roundup of news and links related to buildings, infrastructure, and industrial technology. This week we look at space fiber optic cable manufacturing, nuclear district heating, Spain’s high-speed rail crash, China’s spaceplane, and more. Roughly 2/3rds of the reading list is paywalled, so for full access become a paid subscriber.

An independent committee’s report on the huge Hong Kong apartment complex fire last year found that it was probably started by a lit cigarette, and accelerated by flammable foam boards and scaffolding nets. [BNN Bloomberg]
Bloomberg Philanthropies wants to spread strategies that have helped get housing built in the cities of Atlanta, Austin, and (checks notes) San Diego to other metros in the US. [The New Localism]

Space-based data centers seem to be taking up most of the oxygen for what sort of things become possible if Starship or other technologies makes launch costs much cheaper, but it’s interesting to consider what else might be unlocked from vastly cheaper access to space. Here’s one: incredibly high-quality fiber optic cable. [IEEE Spectrum]

Last week we looked at a report that noted the US produces a very small amount of aluminum, despite our huge demand for it. Apparently one big reason is that we import a large amount of aluminum from Canada, which can produce it thanks to an abundance of cheap hydropower. “...the enormous power requirements for making aluminum have meant that Canada, where abundant hydropower has kept electricity prices from rising as sharply as in the U.S., has supplied about 70% of U.S. aluminum imports in recent years.” [WSJ]
Defense startup Anduril wants to make a laptop in the US. [Anduril]

The Wall Street Journal on the crisis in US explosives manufacturing. “Following the widespread closures of government-owned plants in the 1990s, the entire production of the powerful explosives HMX and RDX came from a single supplier, Holston Army Ammunition Plant. The 84-year-old plant makes about 3% of what it did during peak production in 1944, according to Hacker’s research, and it has been beset by explosions and pollution violations. There is a one- to two-year wait for products coming out of Holston, said industry experts.” [WSJ]

The ultra-competitive Chinese car industry is apparently struggling in the domestic market, thanks to a drop in demand — domestic sales are down 22% compared to last year. This is part of what’s driving the huge export push from Chinese manufacturers. [WSJ]
US utility company First Energy estimates that every 1 GW of data center demand requires about $250 million worth of transmission upgrades. [Utility Dive]
Per Exxon, roughly 10% of global refining capacity is currently offline, mostly refineries in Russia and the Middle East. [Exxon]

blocks.text: Johnston’s Electric Train Shop was a family-owned business in St Louis for about 50 years. As its name suggests, it was a storefront in St Louis’s Dutchtown neighborhood, and advertised itself as St Louis’ first hobby shop that specialized in trains.
But there’s more to the story. This is a classic American Dream story, a small business idea borne of financial hardship that led to owning the building it operated out of and employing 11 people.
Humble beginnings

An article from a 1957 issue of All Aboard, the Lionel corporate newsletter, stated the Johnstons started out selling trains out of their second-floor apartment. It wouldn’t have been an unusual arrangement for them to own the building and rent out the other units, but given he was only 24 years old at the time, they may have been renting. Their daughter-in-law, Pam Johnston, told the same story to the St Louis Post Dispatch in 1974.

According to the 1957 Lionel newsletter article, Eugene and Violet Johnston married December 1, 1928, and he bought two train sets for their first Christmas together. The next year, the stock market crashed and demand for his services as an interior decorator dried up. He passed his time building displays for the trains. Then, at Christmas 1929, he decided to sell the whole setup. His ad brought a crowd to the house and the trains sold immediately. Model Railroader published an abbreviated account from Violet Johnston in 1947, quoting her as saying their business started with the sale of two used electric trains in 1929.
A business borne of necessity

Showing an entrepreneurial streak, Johnston started buying used trains and raw materials for displays with whatever money he could scrounge up. He repaired the trains and built displays to sell at Christmas again.

He left a paper trail that you can still find today. In the early 1930s he ran small classified ads in the St Louis Post-Dispatch offering an electric train for sale, with a phone number. The earliest such ad I could find was in the December 14, 1930 issue of the St Louis Post-Dispatch. The address, 3826 Minnesota Avenue, was a wood shingle multi-family flat in the Dutchtown neighborhood of south St. Louis. In time, the ads offered a selection of trains for sale, and offered trade-ins in addition to straight sales.
The E.R. Johnston Electric Toy Train Co.

Soon, Eugene Johnston developed a reputation as a train expert. He wrote to Lionel asking about selling new trains. Lionel put him in touch with a local distributor. At first he bought trains with profits from the previous day, operating hand to mouth. But soon the business grew larger than they could accommodate out of a second-floor apartment. They set up shop, literally, on the first floor of the apartment building where they lived, with proper counter space, shelves, and a permanent train display. By then, the business employed both Eugene and Violet.

According to a short writeup in the October 1947 issue of Model Railroader, Johnston added scale model railroading in 1935, alongside Lionel tinplate. By May 1939, this included products from William K. Walthers, and Walthers was listing the E.R. Johnston Electric Toy Train Co. as one of its dealers in ads in Model Railroader. Also around 1935, the Johnstons hired their first outside employee.

Surviving photos I’ve seen of the shop interior suggest Eugene Johnston may have built the store fixtures himself from supplies he found at Central Hardware. He would have had the skills to do it. The 1957 All Aboard account noted Eugene and Violet dabbled in rehabilitating real estate on the side.
Johnston’s Electric Train Shop on Chippewa

In mid-1947, a former shoe repair business went up for sale a couple of blocks away from their apartment, at 3118 Chippewa, three miles almost due east of Stan Musial and Biggie’s restaurant on the old Route 66. By October 1947, Johnston’s had moved into this space, and city records suggest the family lived on the second floor. Electric trains became big business after World War II, so it was easy to justify a storefront on a busier street with better visibility. More room and more traffic meant more business and better profits. And living upstairs meant no longer paying rent.

Model Railroader mentioned the move in its October 1947 issue, noting the new address and stating it was one of the few hobby shops in the country that sold model trains exclusively. It said Violet Johnston handled sales while Eugene handled repairs along with one other employee, and they performed 3,320 repairs in 1946.
By the mid 1950s, Johnston’s employed a total of 11 people.

Johnston’s operated out of this storefront, about a mile southwest of where the Cherokee antique district is today, for about three decades. Stories about Johnston’s occasionally pop up in model train forums. The stories include rumors about treasures the family kept in the basement of the building. Apparently the owners encouraged the rumors. Having been buying used trains since 1929, Eugene certainly would have had an opportunity to accumulate a lot of interesting items. It would have been natural to keep some of them.
The second generation of Johnstons selling electric trains

The cover story of Classic Toy Trains October 2004 issue was titled “1956: The Last Perfect Year.” It’s not like Lionel trains went out of style like pet rocks. But demand went into a slow decline in the second half of the decade. The population of the city of St. Louis also started a slow decline around the same time, with middle class families choosing to move to the suburbs.

Eugene Johnston died October 21, 1966, aged 60, at Lutheran Hospital in St. Louis. His wife, Violet Johnston, died March 8, 1974, aged 63, also at Lutheran Hospital. Their son, Korean War veteran Gilbert (Chuck) Johnston and his wife, Pam Beggs Johnston, took over the business.

In a newspaper article about the electric train industry that ran in the December 16, 1974 issue of the St Louis Post Dispatch, Pam Johnston stated they stayed in business selling higher-end trains than the discount stores. They said a significant source of business was people buying a cheap train set from a discounter, the locomotive breaking, and then coming to Johnston’s to buy a more durable replacement.

The implication was that the market for electric trains was declining. And it was. Lionel and Tyco had some success in the 1970s. But it wasn’t the booming business it had been in the 1950s. And in the Johnstons’ case, it didn’t help that hobby shops were opening up elsewhere in the city and in the suburbs. The second-generation Johnstons were living in the suburb of Affton, and commuting seven or eight miles from Affton to an inner city storefront to compete with suburban hobby shops may have contributed to their decision to close the business and get corporate jobs.
Moving on from selling trains

Johnston’s seems to have closed down sometime in 1978. The last advertisement I can find for them ran in the St Louis Post Dispatch in January 1978. Their trail goes cold in Model Railroader earlier than that, after the January 1977 issue. This suggests they may have planned a wind-down of the business, as they would have to purchase advertising in Model Railroader further in advance than in the local newspaper. Their ads in Model Railroader right up to January 1977 used the old-fashioned exchange-style phone number, starting with two letters, which suggests they may have bought the ads years in advance. That convention phased out in the 1960s.

After the store closed, Pam took a job at TWA, the now-defunct airline. Chuck took a job at Anheuser-Busch, running their first computer system. Both of them held those jobs until retirement. Pam died in June 2014, aged 68, and Chuck died in November 2021, aged 88.
Some artifacts from the storefront survive in private collections in St Louis. Rumor is local collectors acquired both the neon signage and the front door.
Final fate

The multifamily flat on Minnesota where a newly married Eugene Johnston sold his train out of desperation, starting a small empire, was demolished in 2003. Minnesota Avenue is mostly a residential street, paved with red bricks, lined with a mix of single and multi-family dwellings. The historic brick homes and red brick street make it easy to imagine what the street looked like a century ago.

The storefront on Chippewa saw heavy turnover after the late 1970s. In the early 2000s, a ramp was added improve accessibility and a recording studio briefly operated out of the space, followed by a computer store.

It changed hands in the early 2020s and was converted to residential use, and in 2022, the current owners pulled a permit to convert the building into a single family residence. When these buildings were built, Chippewa was a busy street through a mixed-use neighborhood, with storefronts near the intersections and pure residential dwellings in between. Changes in  population density, traffic, and modern shopping habits mean there is no longer a need for so many storefronts along Chippewa, so converting some of those turn-of-the-previous-century storefronts to single-family homes means fewer of these old buildings remain vacant.

I saw a reference to Johnston’s in Louis H. Hertz’ 1954 book titled Making Your Model Railroad sometime around 2004. Because I worked very close to that area at the time, I went looking for it. After 25 years, no sign of the former business remained. I wasn’t completely surprised. But I held out faint hope because that area was something of a time capsule back then, with shuttered businesses still leaving traces of themselves behind, sometimes for decades. Not this one, though. The relics had all been salvaged and used to adorn hobbyists’ train rooms. I think that’s better than leaving them to waste away in the elements.

He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.
